# Introduction{-}
Physical systems can often be described by differential equations. A simple example is a system of two identical masses connected by three springs as in @fig-fjedre.

![A system with two identical masses and three identical springs.](figure.svg){width=75% #fig-fjedre fig-alt="Spring system with two masses and three springs"}

We describe the positions of the masses as functions of time by considering $y_1(t)$ and $y_2(t)$ as in the figure, i.e. the positions are the displacements of the masses from the equilibrium position.

When the springs are identical with spring constant $k$, the functions $y_1$ and $y_2$ have to satisfy a system of two second order differential equations, which is derived from Hooke's law and Newton's second law:

$$\begin{align}
  m y_1''(t)&=-2k y_1(t)+k y_2(t), \\
  m y_2''(t)&=k y_1(t) -2k y_2(t).
\end{align}$${#eq-1}

which can be rewritten as
$$\begin{bmatrix}y_1''(t)\\y_2''(t)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{k}{m}\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}y_1(t)\\y_2(t)\end{bmatrix}$$
These equations have to be satisfied for all real numbers $t$. It is thus equations of functions:
$$\begin{bmatrix}y_1''\\y_2''\end{bmatrix}=\frac{k}{m}\begin{bmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\y_2\end{bmatrix}$$

In this assignment, we will use linear algebra to solve such *systems of linear ordinary differential equations*. The following result from e.g. calculus may be considered given:

The set of solutions to $y''=-ay$ with $a>0$ is $$y(t)=c_1\cos(\sqrt{a}t)+c_2\sin(\sqrt{a}t)$$ where $c_1,c_2$ are real numbers.

# Exercise 1{#sec-opg1}
1. Let $B$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix given by 
$$B = \frac{k}{m}
    \begin{bmatrix}
      2 & -1 \\
      - 1 & 2 
    \end{bmatrix}.$$

   Define the column vector
$$\begin{equation*}
    Y(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
      y_1(t) \\
      y_2(t)
    \end{bmatrix}.
  \end{equation*}$$
Show that the system in @eq-1 can be rewritten as $Y''(t)=-BY(t)$.


1. Show that $B$ is orthogonally diagonalizable, i.e. that $B=QDQ^T$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix given by
$$D=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{k}{m}&0\\0&3\frac{k}{m}\end{bmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
Q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}&\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}&-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix},$$
respectively.

1. Now, rewrite the system in @eq-1 as $$(Q^TY)''=-DQ^TY,$$ and let $F=\begin{bmatrix}f_1\\f_2\end{bmatrix}=Q^TY$.

1. Solve the system
$$\begin{equation*}
    \begin{bmatrix}
      f_1\\f_2\end{bmatrix}''=-D\begin{bmatrix}f_1\\f_2\end{bmatrix}
  \end{equation*}$$
and show that
$$\begin{bmatrix}f_1(t)\\f_2(t)\end{bmatrix}
    =\begin{bmatrix}
      c_1\cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}t\right)+c_2\sin\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}t\right)\\
      c_3\cos\left(\sqrt{3\frac{k}{m}}t\right)+c_4\sin\left(\sqrt{3\frac{k}{m}}t\right)
    \end{bmatrix}$${#eq-solution}
	where $c_1,c_2, c_3, c_4$ are real numbers.
   
1. Now, find the solution to the original problem by realizing that $Y(t)=QF(t)$. Also solve the *initial value problem*
$$Y(0)=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0
  \end{bmatrix}$$
  $$Y'(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}$$
  
1. The eigenvectors $V_1=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix}$ and $V_2=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{bmatrix}$ are together with the eigenvalues part of the solution: 
  $$Y(t)=f_1(t)V_1+f_2(t)V_2.$$ 
  (Why?).
  Explain that a solution where $c_3= c_4=0$ corresponds to the situation where the masses oscillate with period $2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$, same amplitude, and in the same direction (in phase). Similarly, the case $c_1=c_2=0$ means that they oscillate with period $2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{3k}}$, same amplitude, and in opposite direction of each other.


# Exercise 2{#sec-opg2}
In this exercise, we investigate the solution in @eq-solution based on the vector space
$$V=\left\{\left[
        \begin{array}{c}
            f\\
            g 
        \end{array}
    \right] : \text{$f$ and $g$ are real functions}\right\},$$
where vector addition and scalar multiplication are defined by
$$\left[\begin{array}{c} f_1\\g_1 \end{array}\right]+
    \left[\begin{array}{c} f_2\\g_2 \end{array}\right]=
    \left[\begin{array}{c} f_1+f_2\\g_1+g_2 \end{array}\right]
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    c\left[\begin{array}{c} f\\g \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c} cf\\cg \end{array}\right].$$
You do not need to show that this is a vector space.

Below, we use the notation
$$\mathbf{b}_1(t)=\left[
        \begin{array}{c}
            \cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}t\right) \\
            0 
        \end{array}
    \right],\quad
    \mathbf{b}_2(t)=\left[
        \begin{array}{c}
            \sin\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}t\right) \\
            0 
        \end{array}
    \right]$$
$$\mathbf{b}_3(t)=\left[
        \begin{array}{c}
            0\\
            \cos\left(\sqrt{3\frac{k}{m}}t\right)
        \end{array}
    \right],\quad
    \mathbf{b}_4(t)=\left[
        \begin{array}{c}
            0\\
            \sin\left(\sqrt{3\frac{k}{m}}t\right)
        \end{array}
    \right]$$

1. Show that any solution of the form @eq-solution lies in $\mathrm{Span}\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3,\mathbf{b}_4\}$.

1. Let $s\neq 0$ be a (fixed) real number. Show that the equality
$$c_1\cos(st)+c_2\sin(st)=0$$
can only be satisfied *for all* $t$ if $c_1=c_2=0$

   ::: {.callout-tip title="Hint" collapse="true"}
   For example, find a $t_1$ such that $\cos(st_1)=1$ and $\sin(st_1)=0$, as well as a $t_2$ such that $\cos(st_2)=0$ and $\sin(st_2)=1$.
   :::
    
1. Conclude from the previous question that $\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3,\mathbf{b}_4\}$ is linearly independent.
    
1. What do the above exercises tell us about $\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3,\mathbf{b}_4\}$ and about the solution set of @eq-1?

1. What is the smallest number of initial conditions for which it is possible to find a unique solution?

# Delopgave 3{#sec-opg3}
The file `animateSolution.py` contains a Python function which shows an animation of the system in @fig-fjedre, when $k$ and $m$ as well as $\mathbf{c}=[c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4]$ are given. In the exercises below, we use $k=m=1$.

::: {.callout-warning title="OBS"}
Currently, the animations from `matplotlib` cannot be run directly in the browser. To see the animation you will therefore need to download the file and run it locally (if you have a Python distribution installed).

Regardless of whether you can run the code or not, you can still solve the initial value problems.
:::

1. First, run the animation for the solution $c_1=c_2=1$ and $c_3=c_4=0$, and then for the solution $c_1=c_2=0$ and $c_3=c_4=1$. Check that the masses oscillate in phase or in antiphase as described in the last part of @sec-opg1.
  
1. Explain why the system of equations for the initial value problem
$$Y(0)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1 \end{bmatrix}
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    Y'\left(\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1 \end{bmatrix}$$
has augmented matrix
$$\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.8}
    \left[
      \begin{array}{cccc|c}
        \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\\
        \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & 0 & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\\
        -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sin(\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}) & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cos(\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}) & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\\
        -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sin(\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}) & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cos(\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}) & 0 & -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\\
      \end{array}
    \right].$$

   Solve the system of equations (you are allowed to use Python or another CAS-tool), and use `animateSolution` to illustrate the solution.
  
1. Finally, consider the initial value problem
$$Y(0)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1 \end{bmatrix}
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    Y(2\pi)=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$$
How many equations and how many unknowns does the system have? How many of these equations involve $c_2$? Is there a unique solution in this case?
